lead: A signal that travels through a channel should come out looking the same, only weaker and a little later. That happens when the channel's gain is flat and its phase is a straight line across the frequencies the signal uses. Such a channel is distortionless. Push the same idea to its limit and you get the ideal filter: perfect gain inside a band, exactly zero outside. Telephone lines, audio amplifiers and radio front ends all aim at these two targets, and both are limits that real hardware only approaches.
prereq: You need: frequency response (magnitude and phase of H(ω)) and the rectangular-pulse and sinc pair of the Fourier transform.

sections.h3: Distortionless transmission: flat gain, straight-line phase

blocks.text: A channel is distortionless when its output is a scaled, delayed copy of its input: y(t) = K x(t − t<sub>d</sub>). K is the gain (a positive constant), t<sub>d</sub> is the delay in seconds, x(t) is the input and y(t) is the output. No new frequencies appear, no shape changes, nothing else happens.

In frequency terms this is two conditions on H(ω), the frequency response. The magnitude must be flat, |H(ω)| = K, and the phase must be a straight line through the origin, ∠H(ω) = −ω t<sub>d</sub>. ω is angular frequency in rad/s. Both conditions must hold over the band the signal occupies, not over all ω.
H(ω) = K e−jω td ⟺ y(t) = K x(t − td)
Here H(ω) is the channel frequency response; K is the constant gain; t<sub>d</sub> is the delay in seconds; the two forms are equivalent for every ω in the signal band.

Break either condition and you get distortion. Amplitude distortion means |H(ω)| is not flat, so some frequencies are scaled more than others; an amplifier with a peak near 3 kHz makes speech sound harsh. Phase distortion means ∠H(ω) is not a straight line, so different frequencies are delayed by different amounts; a pulse sent down a long cable arrives smeared because its high-frequency parts arrive at a different time from its low-frequency parts.

items: Phase delay: t<sub>p</sub> = −∠H(ω)/ω seconds. The time shift felt by the single frequency ω.
Group delay: t<sub>g</sub> = −d∠H(ω)/dω seconds. The time shift felt by a narrow band of frequencies around ω.
For linear phase both equal t<sub>d</sub>, so every frequency is delayed by the same amount.

sections.h3: Ideal filters and the sinc impulse response

blocks.text: An ideal filter passes one band of frequencies with constant gain K and linear phase −ω t<sub>d</sub>, and gives exactly zero gain everywhere else. The magnitude plot looks like a brick wall, so these are called brick-wall filters.

Here h(t) is the impulse response of an ideal low-pass with K = 1 and t<sub>d</sub> = 0; ω<sub>c</sub> is the cut-off in rad/s; sinc(x) = sin(πx)/(πx); the zeros are at t = kπ/ω<sub>c</sub> for k = ±1, ±2, …

The peak is ω<sub>c</sub>/π at t = 0 and the ripples die away only as 1/t. Two consequences follow. First, h(t) is nonzero for t < 0 as well as for t > 0, so the filter is noncausal: it must answer before the input arrives. Second, h(t) never dies out completely, so the filter has infinite memory. A delay t<sub>d</sub> slides the sinc to the right, but the left tail is still infinite, so no finite delay makes it causal. Ideal high-pass and band-stop responses contain a δ(t) term (1 minus the corresponding low-pass brick wall); the ideal band-pass response is the difference of two low-pass brick walls and has no δ(t). All of them are noncausal in the same way.

sections.h3: Why ideal filters cannot be built, and what we build instead

blocks.text: The formal test is the Paley–Wiener condition. If a causal system has an impulse response with finite energy, the integral of |ln|H(ω)|| / (1 + ω²) over all ω must be finite. A band of exact zeros still makes it diverge. Where |H(ω)| = 0 over a band, ln|H| is −∞ there, the integral blows up, and no causal finite-energy system can have that magnitude. Isolated zeros are allowed; a whole band of exact zero is not. So a realisable magnitude may be small, but never exactly zero over a range, and the magnitude plot can never have a truly vertical edge.

Practical filters are therefore specified by tolerances, not by exact equalities. A low-pass specification gives a pass-band edge ω<sub>p</sub> with ripple there (say |H| within ±0.5 dB of K), a stop-band edge ω<sub>s</sub> beyond which |H| stays below a level (say −40 dB), and the transition band from ω<sub>p</sub> to ω<sub>s</sub> between them. Decibels are 20 log₁₀ of a voltage ratio. Group-delay variation across the pass band is specified too, because a filter with flat magnitude can still smear a pulse. Butterworth, Chebyshev and elliptic designs trade ripple against transition sharpness. Some syllabi call this topic distortion-free transmission and realizability of frequency response.

figure.caption: The ideal filter of the worked example: gain 2 inside |ω| ≤ 2000 rad/s, zero outside, and a straight phase line through the origin. The 1000 rad/s input comes out twice as tall and 1 ms later, with its shape unchanged.

spec.aria: Top left: brick-wall magnitude 2 between minus and plus 2000 rad per second. Bottom left: phase line through the origin, minus 1 radian at 1000. Right: input cos 1000t dashed and output 2 cos(1000t minus 1) solid over 0 to 8 ms, shifted by 1 ms.

examples.question: An ideal filter has gain K = 2 and delay t<sub>d</sub> = 1 ms over |ω| ≤ 2000 rad/s, and zero gain outside. The input is x(t) = cos(1000t) V. (a) Check that the input frequency lies in the pass band. (b) Find |H| and ∠H at that frequency. (c) Write y(t). (d) Find y(0).
steps: The input has ω = 1000 rad/s. Since 1000 ≤ 2000, the frequency lies in the pass band, where |H(ω)| = K = 2 and ∠H(ω) = −ω t<sub>d</sub>.
Phase at ω = 1000 rad/s: ∠H = −ω t<sub>d</sub> = −(1000 rad/s)(1 × 10⁻³ s) = −1 rad, which is about −57.3°.
Magnitude at ω = 1000 rad/s: |H| = 2, so the output amplitude is 2 × 1 V = 2 V.
A phase of −1 rad at 1000 rad/s is a time delay of 1 rad ÷ 1000 rad/s = 1 ms, which matches t<sub>d</sub>. So the output is 2 cos(1000t − 1) V.
examples.answer: y(t) = 2 cos(1000t − 1) V, a 2 V wave delayed by 1 ms, and y(0) = 1.0806 V.
examples.check:
import math
K = 2.0
td = 1e-3
w = 1000.0
wc = 2000.0
assert abs(w) <= wc, 'outside pass band'
phase = -w * td
y0 = K * math.cos(phase)
print(round(K, 4))
print(round(phase, 4))
print(round(td, 4))
print(round(y0, 4))

traps: Flat magnitude is not enough. Many answers check |H| = K and stop; a nonlinear phase still distorts the waveform, so both conditions must be checked.
Sign of the phase. A delay gives ∠H = −ω t<sub>d</sub>. Writing +ω t<sub>d</sub> describes an advance, which is noncausal and shifts the signal the wrong way.
Phase delay and group delay are equal only for linear phase. For any other phase they differ, so quoting one when the other is asked loses marks.
Ideal filters are not 'costly but buildable'. No amount of hardware makes them causal; the exact brick wall violates the Paley–Wiener condition.
Distortionless does not mean unity gain. K may be 0.1 or 50; only the flatness of |H| and the linearity of ∠H decide it.

quiz.q: State the two conditions for distortionless transmission and give the resulting input-output relation.
quiz.a: |H(ω)| = K, a constant, and ∠H(ω) = −ω t<sub>d</sub>, a straight line, both over the signal band. Then y(t) = K x(t − t<sub>d</sub>).

quiz.q: Define group delay and give its unit.
quiz.a: t<sub>g</sub> = −d∠H(ω)/dω, in seconds: the delay suffered by a narrow band of frequencies centred at ω.

quiz.q: A channel has |H(ω)| = 1 for all ω but ∠H(ω) = −ω² for |ω| ≤ 100 rad/s. Is it distortionless? Why?
quiz.a: No. The flat magnitude removes amplitude distortion, but the quadratic phase gives a group delay of 2ω s, which changes with frequency. Different components are delayed differently, so the waveform shape changes even though nothing is attenuated.

quiz.q: A distortionless channel has K = 3 and t<sub>d</sub> = 2 ms. The input is 2 cos(500t) V. Find the output.
quiz.a: ω = 500 rad/s is inside the band. |H| = 3, so the amplitude is 3 × 2 = 6 V. ∠H = −(500)(2 × 10⁻³) = −1 rad. Hence y(t) = 6 cos(500t − 1) V.

quiz.q: An ideal low-pass filter has K = 1, t<sub>d</sub> = 0 and cut-off ω<sub>c</sub> = 1000π rad/s. Give h(t), its peak value and its first positive zero.
quiz.a: h(t) = sin(1000πt)/(πt). The peak is at t = 0 with value ω<sub>c</sub>/π = 1000. The first positive zero is at t = π/ω<sub>c</sub> = 1 ms.

quiz.q: An ideal low-pass filter with t<sub>d</sub> = 0 is shifted to t<sub>d</sub> = 5 ms. Is the shifted filter causal? Explain.
quiz.a: No. The shifted response is sin(ω<sub>c</sub>(t − t<sub>d</sub>))/(π(t − t<sub>d</sub>)), which is nonzero for infinitely many t < t<sub>d</sub>, extending without limit to −∞ (in particular there are such points inside 0 < t < t<sub>d</sub>). Any finite shift leaves an infinite left tail, so only t<sub>d</sub> → ∞ would make it causal.

quiz.q: Use the Paley–Wiener condition to explain why a brick-wall stop band is not realisable by a causal finite-energy system.
quiz.a: Over the stop band |H| = 0, so ln|H| = −∞ and the integral of |ln|H||/(1 + ω²) diverges. Paley–Wiener requires that integral to be finite for a causal finite-energy impulse response, so the brick wall is unrealisable. A finite attenuation such as −60 dB is allowed instead.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real designs use Butterworth, Chebyshev and elliptic approximations, and linear-phase FIR digital filters that hold group delay exactly constant across the pass band. A group-delay equaliser is placed after a filter to straighten a curved phase. The Paley–Wiener idea reappears in control theory and in the study of minimum-phase systems. Useful search terms: 'group delay equaliser', 'linear phase FIR', 'Paley–Wiener theorem'.
